newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo cen.bank to convert debt into securities.
newsitem.headline: Yugo cen.bank to convert debt into securities.

text.p: The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) will offer debt relief to the state, banks and firms by converting their debt into securities, a senior central bank official said on Friday.
"NBY plans to convert liabilities of the state, banks and companies into one-year bonds with an interest rate equivalent to the discount rate," NBY Vice-Governor Ratko Banovic told Reuters.
The discount rate stood at a monthly 4.5 percent (68.15 percent a year) in January, unchanged for the eighth consecutive month.
Banovic said the operation was aimed at increasing the number of instruments traded on the financial market, but market analysts feared investor interest could be insignificant.

"They are basically postponing repayment for one year and transforming one form of the debt into another. How can you expect an investor to buy such a paper, if an issuer is obviously unable to repay his debt?" an analyst said.

Banovic would not reveal the size of the debt to be converted into bonds. According to the latest figures issued by the Institute for Market Research, the size of internal debt topped 5.2 billion dinars ($958 million) last November.
The planned conversion of the debt would create two portfolios, one within banks and another within the central bank, Banovic said.

"Companies will have to clear their debt to banks by issuing bonds to their commercial creditors. Based on those securities, banks will issue their own bonds to settle their debt to the central bank," Banovic said.
"But this will not necessarily lead to a direct debt settlement."
There will be two sets of bonds -- one to cover debt based on the principle of extended credits, and another to repay accumulated interest.
"We do not initially expect strong investor interest. But we have to make the first step, to create an instrument and offer it to the market," Banovic said.
Even though there were no legal limits for foreign buyers, NBY expected most interest to come from local investors.
He was confident that bonds would attract more interest in the year of their existence.

"In the entire one-year cycle we expect turnover to increase. Banks and companies will be pushed to work with those securities and on the market. We hope to create a habit of using securities. By the time, banks will probably trace their own interest," Banovic said.

Directing companies and banks to satisfy their borrowing needs on the financial market was a way to ease pressure on the central bank and preventing insolvent banks from expanding their credit activity.
To strengthen financial discipline among banks, NBY has decided to end their malpractice.

"In future, no insolvent bank will be able to extend credits. To qualify for credit activity, a bank must have no outstanding debt, no blocked account, and cannot use funds set aside for the reserve requirement," Banovic said.

Some economists blamed commercial banks for deliberately keeping their balances in the red at the end of 1996, putting pressure on the NBY to print money. This has reflected on the dinar black market rate which plunged to 4.3 to the German mark over the eight-day New Year and Christmas holidays.
The dinar was changing hands at 3.8 before the holidays.
-- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
